section_summary: This section (pages 1-48) of decimal file 894.402 spans February 1941 to November 1944 and documents United States government matters concerning the Japanese language during World War II. It includes correspondence from academics, citizens, and conscientious objectors inquiring about Japanese language training opportunities or offering specialized linguistic services, alongside State Department replies directing applicants to universities and military programs. The file also covers the review and acquisition of Japanese instructional materials, such as Dirk van Hinloopen Labberton's proposed booklets and Vaccari's Kanji cards donated via the Embassy in Santiago, interagency efforts to standardize Japanese military government terminology, and a reference list of Japanese diplomatic titles.

subfiles.about: Hugh Borton requests an interview with Dr. Stanley K. Hornbeck to discuss the efficient mobilization and use of civilian experts in Far Eastern languages during the national emergency.
subfiles.summary: Hugh Borton, Assistant Professor of Japanese at Columbia University, writes to Dr. Stanley K. Hornbeck, Chief of the Far Eastern Division of the Department of State. Acting on suggestions from Professor Knight Biggerstaff of Cornell University and Edward C. Carter of the Institute of Pacific Relations, Borton requests an interview during his upcoming visit to Washington. He emphasizes the need for careful study and sound advice on how civilian specialists in Far Eastern languages and history can best serve during the current emergency. He notes that he can be contacted through the American Council of Learned Societies.
subfiles.title: Letter from Hugh Borton to Stanley K. Hornbeck Requesting an Interview on Utilizing Far Eastern Language Experts

subfiles.about: Dr. Stanley K. Hornbeck agrees to meet with Professor Hugh Borton in Washington to discuss language expertise in the national emergency.
subfiles.summary: Dr. Stanley K. Hornbeck acknowledges Professor Hugh Borton's letter of February 24 regarding the utilization of Far Eastern language specialists. Hornbeck states that he will be pleased to meet with Borton on Thursday afternoon or sometime Friday during Borton's visit to Washington. He asks Borton to telephone his office upon arrival to arrange a mutually convenient appointment time.
subfiles.title: Letter from Stanley K. Hornbeck to Hugh Borton Scheduling an Interview

subfiles.about: Hugh Borton thanks Dr. Stanley K. Hornbeck for agreeing to an interview and confirms that he will telephone upon arriving in Washington.
subfiles.summary: Professor Hugh Borton writes from Columbia University to thank Dr. Stanley K. Hornbeck for offering to grant him an interview. Borton confirms that he will call Hornbeck's office late Thursday or early Friday upon his arrival in Washington to finalize their meeting time. A marginal notation indicates the meeting was scheduled for February 28 at 4:00 p.m.
subfiles.title: Letter from Hugh Borton to Stanley K. Hornbeck Confirming Appointment Arrangements

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing a telegram from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew regarding new Japanese telecommunications regulations affecting language use.
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference file note indexes Telegram No. 996 sent from Tokyo by Ambassador Joseph C. Grew on July 14, 1941. The underlying telegram reports on new Japanese regulations enacted on July 12, 1941, affecting telephone messages and telegrams, specifically providing for the use of Japanese and other foreign languages. The original paper is cross-referenced to decimal file 894.762/1.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference File Note on Japanese Telecommunications Regulations Affecting Language Use

subfiles.about: Maxwell M. Hamilton transmits to Senator Elbert D. Thomas a State Department memorandum evaluating Dr. Dirk van Hinloopen Labberton's proposed Japanese language instructional materials.
subfiles.summary: Maxwell M. Hamilton, Chief of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs, acknowledges receipt of Senator Elbert D. Thomas's letter enclosing Dr. Dirk van Hinloopen Labberton's proposed booklet 'Japanese in One Month' and a sample dictionary page. Hamilton explains that State Department officers with sound knowledge of the Japanese language reviewed the materials and prepared a critical memorandum, which is enclosed. The enclosed memorandum, dated February 11, 1942, concludes that the proposed booklet contains material that could not possibly be mastered in one month and includes unnecessarily difficult grammatical concepts like preterite, desiderative, vetative, and adhortative moods that offer little practical benefit to soldiers. The memorandum also evaluates the sample dictionary page, finding potential practical value but pointing out inaccurate and unidiomatic phrasing.
subfiles.title: Letter from Maxwell M. Hamilton to Senator Elbert D. Thomas with Enclosed Memorandum Evaluating Proposed Japanese Language Materials

subfiles.about: Senator Elbert D. Thomas forwards to the State Department language instructional proposals and sample texts submitted by Dr. Dirk van Hinloopen Labberton.
subfiles.summary: Senator Elbert D. Thomas of Utah transmits to Maxwell M. Hamilton instructional proposals prepared by Dr. Dirk van Hinloopen Labberton to assist American armed forces in learning Japanese. The attached materials include a table of contents for 'Japanese in One Month', an excerpt from a concise Japanese-English dictionary ('Eiwa Sho Ji-biki'), an explanatory note on the importance of the Malay language in the Dutch East Indies, and Labberton's letter of January 18, 1942, to the Naval Intelligence Officer in San Diego. Labberton proposes government subsidies, guaranteed purchases, or outright government publication of his introductory language booklets for the armed services.
subfiles.title: Letter from Senator Elbert D. Thomas to Maxwell M. Hamilton Transmitting Japanese and Malay Language Proposals by Dirk van Hinloopen Labberton

subfiles.about: Eugene H. Lehman Jr., a conscientious objector, offers to study Japanese to serve the government and foster future reconciliation between the United States and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Eugene H. Lehman Jr. of Tarrytown, New York, writes to the Department of State after reading a newspaper report that government agencies intended to sponsor Japanese language courses. Describing himself as an adept language student and an admirer of Japanese culture and literature, Lehman explains that as a conscientious objector, he wishes to serve constructively by mastering the tongue to help rebuild friendly relations after the war. He inquires how he may immediately begin his studies to assist the government.
subfiles.title: Letter from Eugene H. Lehman Jr. to the Department of State Offering to Study Japanese as a Conscientious Objector

subfiles.about: George Atcheson, Jr. informs Eugene H. Lehman Jr. that the State Department has no information on government-sponsored Japanese language courses and suggests contacting universities.
subfiles.summary: George Atcheson, Jr., writing on behalf of the Secretary of State, replies to Eugene H. Lehman Jr.'s inquiry of March 1 regarding reported government-sponsored Japanese language instruction. Atcheson states that the Department is unaware of the basis for the press report and has no knowledge of Japanese courses being offered by any government agency. He advises Lehman that Japanese language courses are offered by several major American universities and suggests inquiring directly with those institutions.
subfiles.title: Letter from George Atcheson, Jr. to Eugene H. Lehman Jr. Regarding Japanese Language Study

subfiles.about: W. G. R. Bishop inquires whether learning Japanese at the University of California would be beneficial for wartime or post-war government service.
subfiles.summary: W. G. R. Bishop of Berkeley, California, writes to Secretary of State Cordell Hull to ask whether it would be advisable to resume studying Japanese for wartime use or post-war reconstruction. Bishop notes that he spent his early youth in Japan and acquired some knowledge of the language, but needs advanced instruction and character study to regain proficiency. Prompted by a radio broadcast regarding language training for government service, he asks if the Department recommends that he enroll in Japanese courses currently being taught at the University of California.
subfiles.title: Letter from W. G. R. Bishop to Secretary of State Cordell Hull Inquiring About Studying Japanese for Government Service

subfiles.about: Robert L. Smyth advises W. G. R. Bishop on government needs for Japanese language specialists and suggests contacting the Civil Service Commission and National Roster.
keywords: National Roster of Scientific and Specialized Personnel
subfiles.summary: Robert L. Smyth, Assistant Chief of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs, replies on behalf of Secretary of State Cordell Hull to W. G. R. Bishop's inquiry of June 29. Smyth explains that while individuals commanding Japanese are scarce and valuable to wartime agencies, the State Department's own needs are fully met by Foreign Service officers who received specialized language training in Japan over many years. He suggests that Bishop contact the Civil Service Commission regarding requirements in other government agencies, and register his qualifications with the National Roster of Scientific and Specialized Personnel once proficient.
subfiles.title: Letter from Robert L. Smyth to W. G. R. Bishop Advising on Opportunities for Japanese Language Speakers

subfiles.about: W. G. R. Bishop thanks the State Department for guidance and confirms his plan to enroll in Japanese language courses at the University of California.
subfiles.summary: W. G. R. Bishop writes to Secretary of State Cordell Hull acknowledging receipt of Assistant Chief Robert L. Smyth's informative letter of July 8. Expressing gratitude for the courteous and prompt reply, Bishop states that the information has encouraged him to pursue mastery of Japanese. He confirms that he plans to attend the University of California in the fall to complete the language course and prepare himself to assist the nation if needed.
subfiles.title: Letter from W. G. R. Bishop to the Secretary of State Expressing Gratitude and Confirming University Enrollment

subfiles.about: Dr. C. P. Rhoads recommends Dr. Kanematsu Sugiura for wartime service where his Japanese language proficiency could be utilized.
subfiles.summary: Dr. Cornelius P. Rhoads, Director of Memorial Hospital for the Treatment of Cancer and Allied Diseases in New York, writes to Under Secretary of State Sumner Welles regarding Dr. Kanematsu Sugiura. Rhoads explains that Dr. Sugiura, a respected hospital staff member who has resided in the United States for over twenty-five years with loyalty established by the FBI, has been forced to stay home due to secret defense research at the hospital. Anxious to contribute to the war effort, Sugiura seeks an opportunity to serve where his knowledge of Japanese would be of value, and Rhoads requests information on potential openings.
subfiles.title: Letter from Dr. C. P. Rhoads to Sumner Welles Regarding War Service for Dr. Kanematsu Sugiura

subfiles.about: Stanley K. Hornbeck informs Dr. C. P. Rhoads that State Department Japanese language needs are filled, suggesting application to the War Department and other wartime agencies for Dr. Sugiura.
subfiles.summary: Dr. Stanley K. Hornbeck, Adviser on Political Relations, replies on behalf of Under Secretary Sumner Welles to Dr. C. P. Rhoads regarding Dr. Kanematsu Sugiura. Hornbeck explains that the State Department's language needs are completely met by specially trained Foreign Service officers, but suggests that Dr. Sugiura might be of valuable service to the War Department, subject to statutory restrictions on employing enemy aliens. He additionally suggests bringing Sugiura's qualifications to the attention of the Federal Communications Commission, Federal Bureau of Investigation, Board of Economic Warfare, and Office of War Information.
subfiles.title: Letter from Stanley K. Hornbeck to Dr. Cornelius P. Rhoads Regarding Potential Employment of Dr. Kanematsu Sugiura

subfiles.about: Fredric J. Becker asks whether intensive study of Japanese history, culture, and language at Columbia University would be valuable for post-war reconstruction.
subfiles.summary: Fredric J. Becker, an advertising executive with Charles W. Hoyt Company in New York, writes to Secretary of State Cordell Hull regarding his intention to undertake an intensive 18-to-24-month program in Japanese language, history, and culture at Columbia University. Becker explains that he hopes such knowledge will serve the armed forces during the war and contribute to post-war reconstruction and lasting peace. He requests the Secretary's views on the post-war necessity and value of American citizens mastering the Japanese tongue.
subfiles.title: Letter from Fredric J. Becker to Secretary of State Cordell Hull Inquiring About Post-War Need for Japanese Language Knowledge

subfiles.about: Robert L. Smyth informs Fredric J. Becker of government language needs and refers him to the Civil Service Commission and National Roster.
keywords: National Roster of Scientific and Specialized Personnel
subfiles.summary: Robert L. Smyth, Assistant Chief of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs, replies on behalf of Secretary Hull to Fredric J. Becker's letter of September 16. Smyth states that while Japanese speakers are scarce and highly valued across government agencies, the State Department's own operational requirements are already fulfilled by Foreign Service officers who received dedicated language training in Japan. He suggests that Becker consult the Civil Service Commission regarding requirements in other government branches, and register his qualifications with the National Roster of Scientific and Specialized Personnel upon completing his studies.
subfiles.title: Letter from Robert L. Smyth to Fredric J. Becker Regarding Japanese Language Proficiency and Government Needs

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing a proposal by George A. Finch for translating untranslated Japanese publications to assist the war effort.
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference file note indexes a letter of October 17, 1942, from George A. Finch of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. The underlying communication transmits a plan for translating untranslated Japanese publications that could contribute to the war effort, and requests the Department's opinion on the initiative. The original paper is cross-referenced to decimal file 740.0011 Pacific War/2871.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference File Note on Translation of Untranslated Japanese Publications

subfiles.about: Gordon Duckworth inquiries whether the State Department offers programs or opportunities for young students to learn the Japanese language.
subfiles.summary: Gordon Duckworth, an eighteen-year-old student at Santa Barbara State College, writes to Under Secretary of State Sumner Welles regarding the scarcity of Japanese speakers in the United States. Noting his aptitude for languages and background in Spanish, Duckworth expresses a strong desire to concentrate all his efforts on mastering Japanese. He asks Welles what opportunities or training programs the State Department offers or might offer in this specialized field.
subfiles.title: Letter from Gordon Duckworth to Sumner Welles Inquiring About Opportunities to Learn Japanese

subfiles.about: The State Department informs Gordon Duckworth that it maintains no language schools and directs him to military schools and major universities.
subfiles.summary: The Department of State replies to Gordon Duckworth's inquiry of November 4 regarding Japanese language training opportunities. The letter clarifies that although the Department previously detailed Foreign Service officers to Japan for language study, it does not currently maintain any instructional courses. The Department indicates that only the War and Navy Departments operate Japanese language schools for their own personnel, and suggests that Duckworth look into courses offered by institutions such as the University of California, Columbia University, and Harvard University.
subfiles.title: Letter from the Department of State to Gordon Duckworth Regarding Japanese Language Training Programs

subfiles.about: Representative Wesley E. Disney transmits an inquiry from Tulsa attorney T. W. Arrington regarding admission to a government Japanese language school in Denver for his son.
subfiles.summary: Representative Wesley E. Disney of Oklahoma forwards to Secretary of State Cordell Hull a letter from Tulsa attorney T. W. Arrington dated November 25, 1942. Arrington explains that his son, an outstanding foreign language student graduating from Tulsa High School, wishes to gain admission to a specialized Japanese language school reportedly established in Denver, Colorado, by the armed services or State Department. Disney requests that the State Department provide whatever information it possesses concerning entrance requirements and the appropriate department to contact.
subfiles.title: Letter from Representative Wesley E. Disney to Cordell Hull Transmitting Inquiry from T. W. Arrington Regarding Military Japanese Language Schools

subfiles.about: Secretary of State Cordell Hull advises Representative Wesley E. Disney that the reported Japanese language school in Colorado is operated by the Navy in Boulder.
subfiles.summary: Secretary of State Cordell Hull replies to Representative Wesley E. Disney's letter of November 30 concerning the inquiry from T. W. Arrington. Hull clarifies that the State Department maintains no language instruction programs, but notes that Arrington likely refers to the Japanese language school operated by the Navy Department in Boulder, Colorado. Hull explains that students at the Boulder school are naval officers or officer candidates, and suggests directing further inquiries to the Navy Department for precise admissions requirements.
subfiles.title: Letter from Cordell Hull to Representative Wesley E. Disney Concerning Navy Japanese Language School in Boulder, Colorado

subfiles.about: George Atcheson, Jr. assures Mrs. C. J. O'Leary that many Americans read Japanese and that former missionaries have already been interviewed by government agencies.
keywords: American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions
subfiles.summary: George Atcheson, Jr. replies on behalf of Secretary Hull to Mrs. C. J. O'Leary's letter of October 20 concerning the alleged scarcity of Japanese speakers in the United States. Atcheson refutes published reports claiming only one hundred people in the country understand Japanese, noting that the State, War, and Navy Departments possess substantial numbers of qualified officers on active duty. He also addresses her recommendation regarding former missionaries, assuring her that numerous former missionaries, including those affiliated with the American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions, have already been interviewed by government agencies for their linguistic qualifications.
subfiles.title: Letter from George Atcheson, Jr. to Mrs. C. J. O'Leary Regarding Japanese Language Proficiency and Former Missionaries

subfiles.about: Mrs. C. J. O'Leary suggests that the State Department recruit former Christian missionaries to Japan who possess fluent Japanese language skills.
keywords: American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions
subfiles.summary: Mrs. C. J. O'Leary of Santa Monica, California, writes to Secretary of State Cordell Hull after reading an article claiming that only one hundred individuals in the United States understand and read Japanese. She asks whether the State Department has considered utilizing former missionaries who lived with Japanese families and studied the language for years. Acknowledging that missionaries might hesitate to volunteer because they view the Japanese people as friends rather than enemies, she argues that national preservation requires utilizing all talents, and provides the address of the American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions in Boston to facilitate contact.
subfiles.title: Letter from Mrs. C. J. O'Leary to Secretary of State Cordell Hull Suggesting Utilization of Former Missionaries to Japan

subfiles.about: H. Merrell Benninghoff suggests obtaining and retaining in the library a set of Chinese-Japanese character cards reported by the Embassy in Santiago.
subfiles.summary: H. Merrell Benninghoff of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs submits a memorandum to Edward G. Barber regarding Santiago's Airgram No. A-625 concerning a set of Chinese-Japanese character cards. Benninghoff notes that the Division is familiar with the cards and, while not urgently needed by Far Eastern Affairs, suggests they be obtained and placed in the library or another suitable repository. He leaves the decision of whether the Department should purchase the cards to the Division of Research and Publication.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from H. Merrell Benninghoff to Edward G. Barber Regarding Chinese-Japanese Character Cards

subfiles.about: The Division of Research and Publication reports on the commercial availability of Vaccari Kanji cards and recommends accepting them only as a gift.
subfiles.summary: The Division of Research and Publication submits a brief internal memorandum regarding the Vaccari Kanji cards referenced in Santiago's Airgram No. A-625. The memorandum notes that the cards can be purchased commercially in the United States for $7.50, meaning government purchase through the Embassy in Santiago is unnecessary. It concludes, however, that the Department might accept the cards if the donor is willing to present them as a gift.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from the Division of Research and Publication Regarding Acquisition of Vaccari Kanji Cards

subfiles.about: The American Embassy in Santiago reports that anti-Nazi German resident Albert Thiele has offered a complete set of primary school Kanji cards for donation or purchase.
subfiles.summary: The American Embassy in Santiago transmits Airgram No. A-625 to the Secretary of State, reporting that Mr. Albert Thiele, an anti-Nazi German residing in Chile, possesses a complete set of Chinese-Japanese primary school character cards prepared by Mr. and Mrs. Oreste Vaccari ('An Easy Method to Learn Kanji'). The Embassy reports that Thiele has offered the cards, expressing a preference that they be donated or sold to an American military institute engaged in teaching Oriental languages. The Embassy requests instructions on whether the Department wishes to acquire the set by purchase or accept it as a gift.
subfiles.title: Airgram No. A-625 from American Embassy, Santiago Concerning Donation of Kanji Character Cards by Albert Thiele

subfiles.about: Ambassador Claude G. Bowers transmits to the State Department a set of primary school Kanji cards donated by anti-Nazi German resident Albert Thiele.
subfiles.summary: United States Ambassador Claude G. Bowers in Santiago transmits Despatch No. 6712 to the Secretary of State, forwarding a complete set of Chinese-Japanese primary school character cards titled 'An Easy Method to Learn Kanji', authored by Mr. and Mrs. Oreste Vaccari. Bowers explains that the donor, Mr. Albert Thiele, is an anti-Nazi German residing in Chile who presents the material as a gift. Bowers notes Thiele's wish that the instructional set be placed with an American military institute engaged in teaching Oriental languages.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 6712 from Claude G. Bowers to Secretary of State Transmitting "An Easy Method to Learn 'Kanji'"

subfiles.about: The State Department instructs the American Embassy in Santiago that it will accept Albert Thiele's Kanji cards only as a gift.
subfiles.summary: Secretary of State Cordell Hull sends Airgram No. 861 to the American Embassy in Santiago responding to Airgram No. A-625 of May 8 regarding the character cards comprising 'An Easy Method to Learn Kanji'. Hull instructs the Embassy that the Department does not consider it necessary to purchase the set from Mr. Albert Thiele. He indicates, however, that the Department will be glad to accept the instructional cards if Mr. Thiele wishes to present them as an outright gift.
subfiles.title: Airgram No. 861 from Cordell Hull to American Embassy, Santiago Regarding Acceptance of Kanji Cards as Gift

subfiles.about: The State Department instructs the American Mission in Santiago to convey the War Department's appreciation to Albert Thiele for his gift of Kanji character cards.
subfiles.summary: Secretary of State Cordell Hull transmits Instruction No. 3471 to the Officer in Charge of the American Mission in Santiago regarding Despatch No. 6712 of June 9. The instruction encloses a memorandum of September 10 from the War Department gratefully acknowledging receipt of Albert Thiele's donation of 'An Easy Method to Learn Kanji'. Hull requests that the Mission transmit an appropriate acknowledgment of thanks to Mr. Thiele for making the valuable instructional set available for military training.
subfiles.title: Instruction No. 3471 from Cordell Hull to American Mission, Santiago Requesting Acknowledgment of Gift to Albert Thiele
subfiles.to: Officer in Charge of the American Mission, Santiago

subfiles.about: The State Department Liaison Officer transmits Albert Thiele's gift of Kanji cards to the Military Intelligence Service of the War Department.
subfiles.summary: The State Department Liaison Officer sends a memorandum to Major Ward E. Miller, Military Intelligence Service Liaison Officer with the State Department, enclosing a copy of Santiago's Despatch No. 6712. The memorandum forwards the set of primary school Chinese-Japanese character cards ('An Easy Method to Learn Kanji') donated by Mr. Albert Thiele. The Liaison Officer notes Thiele's request that the set be presented to a military institute teaching Oriental languages, and offers to relay any statement the War Department desires to make regarding its usefulness.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from State Department Liaison Officer to Major Ward E. Miller Transmitting "An Easy Method to Learn 'Kanji'"

subfiles.about: The Military Intelligence Service acknowledges receipt of Albert Thiele's Kanji cards and confirms they will be used to instruct military personnel.
subfiles.summary: Colonel William Mayer, G.S.C., Acting Chief of the Pacific Unit in the Military Intelligence Service of the War Department, sends a memorandum to the State Department Liaison Officer regarding Albert Thiele's gift. Mayer gratefully acknowledges receipt of the character cards transmitted by the Embassy in Santiago. He reports that the set is extremely helpful for learning Japanese characters and will be utilized to good advantage in teaching Japanese to military personnel within the Military Intelligence Division, requesting that formal thanks be forwarded to the donor.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from Colonel William Mayer to State Department Liaison Officer Acknowledging Receipt of Kanji Cards

subfiles.about: Abbot Low Moffat proposes establishing an interagency committee to agree upon uniform Japanese translations for American military government terminology.
subfiles.summary: Abbot Low Moffat, Adviser in the Liberated Areas Division of the Department of State, writes to Major General John H. Hilldring, Director of the War Department's Civil Affairs Division. Moffat points out that translating American technical terms into Japanese is difficult and experts frequently reach divergent conclusions. He emphasizes that uniform and accurate Japanese terminology is critical for military government operations across the Army, Navy, Treasury, FEA, State Department, and OWI, and requests that General Hilldring designate an Army representative to meet with State Department officials to establish agreed standard translations.
subfiles.title: Letter from Abbot Low Moffat to Major General John H. Hilldring Proposing Standardization of Japanese Military Government Terminology

subfiles.about: Captain Wallace S. Wharton transmits to Frederick B. Lyon a reference list of Japanese diplomatic titles and administrative terms from the 1937 Foreign Office Year Book.
subfiles.summary: Captain Wallace S. Wharton, U.S.N.R., of the Office of the Chief of Naval Operations, transmits to Frederick B. Lyon of the Department of State an enclosed reference memorandum dated November 27, 1944, on Japanese diplomatic terms. The enclosed five-page compilation reproduces commonly used Japanese administrative and diplomatic titles alongside their English equivalents as published in the 1937 Japanese Foreign Office Year Book (Gaimusho Gankan). The list includes Romanized Japanese terms for ministerial positions, embassies, consulates, bureau directorships, diplomatic ranks, and specialized clerical designations.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from Captain Wallace S. Wharton to Frederick B. Lyon Transmitting Compilation of Japanese Diplomatic Terms
